doc.title: Ken Peplowski interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Not treating music as a job; Goodman's attitude
summary: Commitment to playing, and Goodman refusing nostalgia for Harry James and Krupa.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: Yeah. But that’s the thing. You know if you’re going to play music, if you’ve made this commitment, the worst thing you can do for yourself is treat it like a job and show up — © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

like these kind of things — we’re on a jazz party right now. It’s very easy to just go and play the same old tunes. And a lot of people do, to be honest, and get very lazy about it. But it’s not worth my while personally to get up there and just go through the motions. Even if I’m playing somebody else’s same old tune, I’m trying to play some music, for good or for bad. I’m not saying I’m a great musician but at least I try. Otherwise there’s no point to playing music. You could be doing something else and making a lot more money and having a bigger reward and you learn that by being around people like him. Up to the end he was practicing, he was still excited about playing “Stealing Apples” you know, and it meant a lot to him. It was never a nostalgic trip with him. In fact he would get very angry if people wanted to talk about the good old days with Harry James and Gene Krupa. He’d say, “hey I don’t want to talk about them, I want to talk about the band I have now.”
